cues.text: A Frail Girl with a Fixed Purpose
Born in 1850 at Sant'Angelo Lodigiano, near Lodi in northern Italy, Maria Francesca Cabrini was the youngest of thirteen children.
Only four survived to adulthood.
As a young girl, she resolved to devote her life to religious work, even privately vowing herself to virginity at twelve.
Twice she sought admission to religious orders and was twice refused — her health, weakened by a childhood bout of smallpox contracted while nursing the sick, judged too fragile for convent life.
Founding Her Own Order
Undeterred, Frances took charge of an orphanage in Codogno, and when it closed in 1880, the local bishop asked her to gather the orphaned girls she had trained into a new religious community.
She did so, founding the Missionary Sisters of the Sacred Heart of Jesus and taking the name Xavier in honor of the great Jesuit missionary Francis Xavier .
He was the very model of the missionary vocation she still hoped, one day, to pursue herself in China.
'Not to the East, but to the West'
When Frances traveled to Rome to seek Pope Leo XIII's blessing for a mission to China, he redirected her toward a mission closer to home.

It was no less urgent: tens of thousands of poor Italian immigrants were arriving in the United States, often facing discrimination, exploitation, and neglect from the wider American Catholic Church itself.
'Not to the East, but to the West,' the pope told her, and Frances obeyed, sailing for New York with six sisters in 1889.
Building an Empire of Charity
Arriving to find that the house intended for her first orphanage had fallen through entirely, Frances met one disappointment after another in her early American years.

Yet within a remarkably short time, her order's work expanded into a vast network of schools, orphanages, and hospitals serving Italian immigrant communities, eventually spreading beyond the United States into South America and Europe as well.
An American Citizen
Frances became a naturalized United States citizen in 1907.
By the time of her death, she had personally founded some sixty-seven institutions across two continents.
She traveled tirelessly by ship despite a lifelong fear of drowning stemming from a childhood accident, crossing the Atlantic some thirty times over the course of her ministry.
Legacy
Frances died at her own Columbus Hospital in Chicago in 1917, and was canonized in 1946 by Pope Pius XII — the first citizen of the United States ever declared a saint.
Named patron of immigrants in 1950, her enduring legacy is carried on by the many schools and hospitals she founded.
It also lives through the Missionary Sisters of the Sacred Heart, still active today in fifteen countries, honoring a woman twice told she was too frail for religious life.
She went on to build an institutional empire of charity spanning two hemispheres.
